name: User Retention
contentMarkdown:
# User Retention

User retention measures how many people in a starting group return to use a product over time. A retention rate uses a defined group, a return behavior, and a time window. For a product used by teams, the same approach can measure retention at the account level.

## How do you calculate a retention rate?

**Retention rate = eligible cohort members who meet the return condition ÷ all eligible members of the starting cohort × 100.**

A cohort is a group that shares a starting condition, such as signing up in the same week. Define what counts as returning, then give every cohort member the full observation window. Choose a return event that reflects the product’s job, such as sending an invoice for an invoicing tool.

## Example of account retention

An invoicing team wants to know whether new accounts keep using the product after initial activation. The cohort includes 120 eligible new accounts that sent their first real invoice within seven days of signup. The return condition is sending another real invoice during days 15–30 after signup.

If 72 of those accounts meet the return condition, the **retention rate for this activated cohort is 60%** (72 ÷ 120 × 100). Count each account once, even if its team sends several invoices. Read the result after all accounts have finished day 30.

To compare later use across activated and non-activated accounts, use a return condition both can meet. Sending any real invoice during days 15–30 works for that question. It answers a different question from repeat use among accounts that already sent an invoice.

## Which time window should you use?

Match the window to the natural usage cycle. A daily collaboration tool and a monthly invoicing product can show very different patterns. Day-30 retention counts a return on that day. A days 15–30 window counts any qualifying return in that interval. For “day 30 or later,” state the reporting cutoff and give cohorts comparable follow-up time.

Read retention alongside [activation](/glossary/activation-metric.html). Activation tracks initial progress. Retention tracks a return to meaningful work. A drop in usage retention can prompt investigation into who stopped returning and why. Subscription churn measures a separate outcome, such as cancellation or nonrenewal.

## Related terms

- [Activation Metric](/glossary/activation-metric.html)
- [Time-to-Value (TTV)](/glossary/time-to-value-ttv.html)
- [North Star Metric (NSM)](/glossary/north-star-metric-nsm.html)
- [Churn Mitigation Architecture](/glossary/churn-mitigation-architecture.html)

name: Product-Qualified Lead (PQL)
contentMarkdown:
# Product-Qualified Lead (PQL)

A product-qualified lead (PQL) is a prospective buyer whose product use provides evidence that they may be ready to purchase. Teams combine usage with customer fit and intent to decide whether to offer help, route the lead to sales, or keep the experience self-service.

## How is a PQL different from activation or an MQL?

An [activation event](/glossary/activation-metric.html) indicates initial product value. A PQL rule identifies a prospect for a commercial next step. A marketing-qualified lead (MQL) is qualified primarily through marketing engagement and fit. The same person may qualify through more than one route.

## Example for a team planning tool

A planning product offers one shared project for free. A team activates when two teammates complete their first shared task. Several weeks later, an administrator requests help enabling controls available on the paid plan. The workspace shows evidence of account-level fit and usage. The administrator’s request gives the team a specific person to help and a reason to follow up.

| Signal | Example |
|---|---|
| Product use | Teammates complete shared tasks and return to do more work. |
| Fit | The team needs controls the paid plan supports. |
| Intent | A workspace administrator asks about enabling those controls. |
| Next step | Answer the question or offer a setup conversation when appropriate. |

In a team product, decide whether the rule qualifies an individual or an account. Account-level qualification is often called a **product-qualified account (PQA)**. The workspace may show the usage signal while a specific administrator is the appropriate contact.

## How do you validate a PQL rule?

Write the events, qualifying conditions, time window, and unit before comparing results. Check whether flagged prospects go on to buy at a higher rate than comparable eligible prospects. Review false positives, such as active users who have no purchasing role or teams that are well served by the free plan.

Evaluate outreach separately from the rule. For example, if there is enough traffic, randomly assign eligible qualified prospects to an offer of help or the usual experience and compare paid conversion. Keep qualification tied to a useful next step and respect the customer’s contact preferences.

## Related terms

- [Product-Led Growth (PLG)](/glossary/product-led-growth-plg.html)
- [Activation Metric](/glossary/activation-metric.html)
- [Lead Capture](/glossary/lead-capture-mechanics.html)
- [Product Telemetry & Analytics](/glossary/product-telemetry-analytics.html)

name: AI Unit Economics
contentMarkdown:
# AI Unit Economics

AI unit economics is the analysis of revenue and costs for a defined unit of an AI product, such as a customer account or a completed task. Task-level analysis includes model use, tools, retries, failed runs, and any human work within the stated cost boundary.

## What is the unit in an AI product?

Choose an account, workflow, or task that matches the decision. A model call is not necessarily a completed task: extracting one correct invoice record may require several calls and a human check.

Define success before calculating cost. For invoice extraction, acceptance might require the right supplier, date, currency, and total, checked against the source document. Producing valid JSON alone does not establish correctness.

## How do you calculate cost per successful task?

For a defined group of tasks with a complete observation window:

**Cost per successful task = total stated workflow costs ÷ tasks meeting the success criteria.**

Include costs from failed, abandoned, and retried tasks in the numerator. Count each accepted task once. State whether a task completed by a human counts as a success, and include that human work when it does.

This is an operational measure with a declared cost boundary, not a universally standardized accounting ratio. If no tasks succeed, the average cost per success is undefined.

## An AI unit economics example

Consider an illustrative invoice workflow with 1,000 submitted tasks. After retries and review, 800 produce accepted records within the observation window.

| Cost pool for all 1,000 tasks | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Model inference across all attempts | $120 |
| Retrieval, tools, and allocated infrastructure | $30 |
| Human checking and correction | $50 |
| Total stated workflow cost | $200 |

- Cost per submitted task = $200 ÷ 1,000 = **$0.20**.
- Cost per successful task = $200 ÷ 800 = **$0.25**.

If those 800 accepted tasks generate $400 in attributable revenue, $200 remains after this cost pool. That subtotal still excludes acquisition, product development, and any other unmodeled expenses; it is not automatically company net profit.

A variant that costs $150 but produces only 500 accepted tasks costs $0.30 per success. Compare variants on the same workload and acceptance rules.

## Why is token price insufficient?

Provider bills can distinguish input and output tokens, cache writes and reads, and paid tools. Additional attempts and growing context can change the number of billable units.

Use actual workflow measurements, including human effort, and reconcile estimates with billing data. A lower token rate does not establish a lower cost per accepted result.

When tasks span reporting periods, use a consistent task cohort or account for work still in progress. Dividing this month's costs by this month's completions can misalign work and outcomes.

## What should product designers influence?

Investigate the behavior behind costly runs:

- Help users supply the required source information.
- Let users revise the affected part rather than repeat the entire workflow.
- Explain an estimate and obtain confirmation before expensive work where appropriate.
- Provide a usable recovery or human handoff when automation fails.

Measure acceptance, rework, latency, and service effort alongside cost. A design that reduces calls but leaves more work for customers has shifted effort rather than necessarily improved the outcome.

Connect the findings to [pricing](/glossary/pricing-metric.html) and [cost to serve](/glossary/cost-to-serve.html). An internal successful-task definition may differ from an [outcome-based pricing](/glossary/outcome-based-pricing.html) contract's billable event.

## Related terms

- [Cost to Serve](/glossary/cost-to-serve.html)
- [Gross Margin](/glossary/gross-margin.html)

name: CAC Payback Period
contentMarkdown:
# CAC Payback Period

CAC payback period is the time required to recover customer acquisition cost from the value generated by acquired customers. The gross-margin-adjusted SaaS measure used here tracks recovery through gross profit and expresses the period in months.

## What is the CAC payback formula?

For a simplified subscription model:

**CAC payback in months = CAC ÷ (average monthly revenue per account × gross margin percentage).**

The denominator is monthly gross profit per account. Use the same customer definition and cost boundary as your [CAC](/glossary/customer-acquisition-cost-cac.html) and [LTV](/glossary/customer-lifetime-value-ltv.html) calculations.

This shortcut assumes the account continues paying and produces stable monthly gross profit. It does not model cancellations, a gradual increase in usage, or changes in delivery costs.

If monthly gross profit is zero or negative, there is no finite payback under the unchanged assumptions. A negative arithmetic result is not a negative recovery time.

## A SaaS payback example

An illustrative business spends $100,000 to acquire 100 paying accounts. Each account generates $100 in monthly revenue with $20 in cost of revenue.

| Calculation | Result |
|---|---:|
| CAC: $100,000 ÷ 100 | $1,000 |
| Monthly gross profit per account: $100 − $20 | $80 |
| Gross margin: $80 ÷ $100 | 80% |
| Simplified payback: $1,000 ÷ $80 | 12.5 months |

With monthly contributions posted at month-end, the account crosses the $1,000 threshold in month 13 if it remains a customer.

Dividing $1,000 by $100 gives 10 months, but that revenue-only calculation leaves out delivery costs. Label the basis whenever comparing payback figures.

## How do you account for churn and changing usage?

Track the acquired cohort as a group. For each month after acquisition, subtract that cohort's cost of revenue from its revenue. Add the monthly gross profit until the cumulative total reaches the cohort's original acquisition spending.

Keep accounts that cancel in the original cohort; their later contribution is zero. Averaging only surviving customers makes recovery appear faster.

In the example, 2% monthly customer churn means the cohort will not keep generating its initial $8,000 of gross profit each month. A model that includes those departures therefore gives a longer payback than the 12.5-month shortcut, assuming the other inputs stay unchanged.

For usage-based products, track changing consumption and costs directly. If AI usage increases revenue while also increasing delivery costs, additional revenue alone does not establish faster payback.

## CAC payback vs. LTV:CAC

[LTV:CAC](/glossary/ltv-to-cac-ratio.html) compares estimated lifetime value with acquisition cost. Payback measures how quickly acquisition cost is recovered.

Two products can have the same lifetime ratio and different payback periods. If each has $1,000 CAC and $4,000 estimated gross-profit LTV, one might generate $80 monthly gross profit while another generates $40 over a longer customer relationship.

A favorable lifetime ratio can still leave a long period before acquisition spending is recovered.

## What is a good CAC payback period?

There is no universal target. Customer segment, retention, margin, sales cycle, and available cash all affect interpretation.

Compare the same calculation across comparable cohorts. Check whether customers tend to leave before acquisition spending is recovered, and whether the business can fund the intervening costs.

Annual upfront billing changes cash collection timing. It does not make a year of gross profit earned immediately; distinguish cash recovery from the gross-profit payback measure used here.

## How can product designers use payback?

Investigate delays between acquisition and paid value: incomplete setup, failed first tasks, or confusing upgrades. Measure whether a change helps appropriate accounts reach sustained paid use, with support costs and cancellations included.

An interface that pushes an unsuitable annual commitment might improve cash collection while increasing refunds or distrust. Assess the whole customer outcome before interpreting a shorter cash-recovery period as a product improvement.

## Related terms

- [Unit Economics](/glossary/unit-economics.html)
- [Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)](/glossary/customer-acquisition-cost-cac.html)
- [Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)](/glossary/customer-lifetime-value-ltv.html)
- [LTV to CAC Ratio](/glossary/ltv-to-cac-ratio.html)
- [Time-to-Value (TTV)](/glossary/time-to-value-ttv.html)

name: Contribution Margin
contentMarkdown:
# Contribution Margin

Contribution margin is revenue minus variable costs. It shows how much remains to cover fixed costs and, once those costs are covered, contribute to operating profit. It can be expressed as a total amount, an amount per unit, or a percentage of revenue.

## What are the contribution margin formulas?

- **Total contribution margin = total revenue − total variable costs.**
- **Contribution per unit = revenue per unit − variable cost per unit.**
- **Contribution margin ratio = contribution margin ÷ revenue × 100.**

State the unit and time period. One order, one active account-month, and one completed task are different units.

Variable costs change with the relevant activity. Fixed costs remain unchanged within a stated activity range and period. A salaried support team, for example, does not necessarily cost less immediately because a workflow generates fewer tickets.

## A SaaS contribution margin example

Consider one illustrative active account-month, with these documented cost classifications:

| Item | Amount | Treatment in this example |
|---|---:|---|
| Revenue | $100 | Revenue for the month. |
| Variable delivery costs | $12 | Included in cost of revenue. |
| Allocated fixed delivery costs | $8 | Included in cost of revenue, excluded from variable costs. |
| Recurring partner commission | $5 | Variable selling expense outside cost of revenue. |

**Contribution per account-month = $100 − $12 − $5 = $83.**

**Contribution margin ratio = $83 ÷ $100 × 100 = 83%.**

At 100 equivalent account-months, total contribution is $8,300 before fixed costs. This is not $8,300 of net profit.

The $5 commission is an ongoing monthly expense in this example. If acquisition spending is evaluated elsewhere in the model, reconcile the cost pools to avoid subtracting the same commission twice.

## Why can contribution margin differ from gross margin?

Using the same example, cost of revenue is $12 + $8 = $20. [Gross profit](/glossary/gross-margin.html) is therefore $80 and gross margin is 80%.

Contribution is $83 because it excludes the $8 fixed allocation but includes the $5 variable commission. The higher percentage does not mean the business earned extra money. It means the two measures subtract different cost categories.

For internal decisions, list every included cost rather than relying on a label such as “margin after costs.” If you remove only selected variable costs, name that narrower subtotal clearly.

## How does contribution margin inform product decisions?

Suppose a workflow consumes a paid third-party check on every submission. A clearer preview might help users correct mistakes before submitting, reducing unnecessary checks.

Measure successful submissions, repeated checks, and the variable cost per completed task. Include the implementation effort and any new fixed expenses in the broader decision.

With positive contribution, additional volume helps cover fixed costs under unchanged assumptions. With negative contribution, each additional unit increases the shortfall. That conclusion depends on prices, costs, and capacity remaining as modeled; growth may require new capacity.

## What should designers avoid?

Do not treat every allocated cost as an immediate saving. Reducing support work can free capacity while payroll remains unchanged. Report the capacity benefit separately from cash savings.

Also check customer outcomes. Blocking legitimate retries or making support harder to reach can reduce a visible cost while leaving users unable to complete their work.
